title: Server-side sessions
summary: HTTP forgets you after every request. A session id remembers you, if it is random enough and expires properly.

steps.title: HTTP forgets
body: HTTP is **stateless**: every request stands alone. After `POST /login` succeeds, the next request, `GET /account`, arrives with no memory of it. The server needs a way to recognise the same user again without asking for the password every time.
The classic answer is a **server-side session**:
```text
POST /login  (username + password)
server: password ok -> make a random id "9f2c...", store  9f2c... -> { user: "ada", created, lastSeen }
response: Set-Cookie: sid=9f2c...
GET /account
Cookie: sid=9f2c...
server: look up 9f2c... -> ada

The browser holds only a meaningless random **session id**. Everything that matters (who the user is, when they logged in) stays on the server. That has a big advantage you will appreciate in the JWT module: to log someone out, you delete one row.

steps.prompt: In a server-side session design, what does the cookie contain?
options: Only an unguessable random id that points at the server's session record
The username and a flag saying the user is logged in
The password hash, so the server can re-check it on every request
The user's roles, so the server doesn't need to look them up
steps.explain: Anything in a cookie can be read and edited by the user. Put `user=ada; admin=true` in a cookie and someone will change it to `user=root`. A random id is useless to change: the attacker would have to guess another live id.

steps.title: Making a session id
body: A session id is a password that the server hands out. Whoever presents it *is* that user, so it must be impossible to guess:
- Take it from a **cryptographically secure** random source: `RandomNumberGenerator`.
- Make it long: at least **128 bits**. 256 bits is common and costs nothing.
- It must carry **no meaning**: no username, no timestamp, no counter.
```csharp
using System.Security.Cryptography;
string id = Convert.ToHexString(RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32));  // 256 bits, 64 hex characters
// or: RandomNumberGenerator.GetHexString(64)
`System.Random` is **not** acceptable: it is a fast predictable generator for games and simulations, and its future output can be worked out from a few samples.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (The random bytes differ every run; the lengths do not.)
steps.explain: Hex uses 2 characters per byte. Base64 uses 4 characters for every 3 bytes, rounded up with padding: 32 bytes need 44 characters. 16 bytes are 128 bits.

steps.prompt: Would each one make an acceptable session id?
items: The next number from a database sequence
SHA-256 of the username and login time
steps.explain: Sequences and timestamps are guessable, `Random` is predictable, and a hash of guessable inputs is still guessable: an attacker hashes the same inputs.

steps.title: Sessions must end
body: A session that lives forever is a stolen session that works forever. Use two timeouts together:
- **Idle timeout**: end the session after, say, 20 minutes without a request. Each request moves `lastSeen` forward (a *sliding* expiry).
- **Absolute timeout**: end it after, say, 8 hours since login **no matter what**. Otherwise a session kept busy by an attacker (or by a script) slides forever.
```csharp fragment
bool Expired(Session s, DateTimeOffset now) =>
now - s.LastSeen >= IdleTimeout || now - s.Created >= AbsoluteTimeout;
When a session has expired, delete it and treat the request as unauthenticated (`401`). Banks use short timeouts; a chat app may use long ones. The point is that both exist.

steps.prompt: Complete the check: idle for 20 minutes, or 8 hours since login.
code: bool Expired(DateTimeOffset created, DateTimeOffset lastSeen, DateTimeOffset now) =>
steps.explain: Either limit ends the session, so the two conditions are joined with `||`.

steps.prompt: Why keep an absolute timeout when you already have an idle timeout?
options: A session in constant use would otherwise never expire, so a stolen one could be kept alive indefinitely
Idle timeouts don't work with cookies
Absolute timeouts make sessions faster to look up
They are the same thing with different names

steps.title: A session store
prompt: Write a class `SessionStore` that keeps sessions in memory.
- `string Create(string user, DateTimeOffset now)`: makes a new 256-bit random id (as 64 hex characters), stores the session, returns the id.

- `string? GetUser(string id, DateTimeOffset now)`: returns the user, or `null` when the id is unknown or the session has expired (idle **or** absolute, using `>=`). An expired session is removed. A successful lookup moves the idle clock forward to `now`.
The tests already import `System.Security.Cryptography`; don't add `using` lines.
starter: public string Create(string user, DateTimeOffset now) => "";
public string? GetUser(string id, DateTimeOffset now) => null;
solution: public string Create(string user, DateTimeOffset now)
_sessions[id] = new Session { User = user, Created = now, LastSeen = now };
public string? GetUser(string id, DateTimeOffset now)
if (!_sessions.TryGetValue(id, out var s)) return null;
hints: Store a small class with `User`, `Created` and `LastSeen` in a `Dictionary<string, ...>`.
In `GetUser`, check both timeouts, remove on expiry, otherwise set `LastSeen = now`.
template: using System.Security.Cryptography;
var dojoT0 = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 1, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
var dojoS = new SessionStore(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20), TimeSpan.FromHours(8));
var dojoId = dojoS.Create("ada", dojoT0);
Dojo.Eq("the id is 64 characters", 64, dojoId.Length);
Dojo.Check("the id is hex", dojoId.All(Uri.IsHexDigit), dojoId);
Dojo.Check("two ids differ", dojoS.Create("ada", dojoT0) != dojoId, "the same id came back twice");
Dojo.Eq("lookup right away", "ada", dojoS.GetUser(dojoId, dojoT0));
Dojo.Eq("unknown id -> null", null, dojoS.GetUser("not-an-id", dojoT0));
Dojo.Eq("after 19 minutes idle: still valid", "ada", dojoS.GetUser(dojoId, dojoT0.AddMinutes(19)));
Dojo.Eq("19 minutes after that request: still valid (sliding)", "ada", dojoS.GetUser(dojoId, dojoT0.AddMinutes(38)));
Dojo.Eq("20 minutes idle: expired", null, dojoS.GetUser(dojoId, dojoT0.AddMinutes(58)));
Dojo.Eq("expired sessions stay gone", null, dojoS.GetUser(dojoId, dojoT0.AddMinutes(59)));
var dojoBusy = dojoS.Create("grace", dojoT0);
string? dojoLast = null;
for (int m = 10; m < 8 * 60; m += 10) dojoLast = dojoS.GetUser(dojoBusy, dojoT0.AddMinutes(m));
Dojo.Eq("a busy session is valid at 7h50m", "grace", dojoLast);
Dojo.Eq("but ends at 8 hours (absolute)", null, dojoS.GetUser(dojoBusy, dojoT0.AddHours(8)));
var dojoGone = dojoS.Create("bob", dojoT0);
dojoS.Remove(dojoGone);
Dojo.Eq("a removed session is gone", null, dojoS.GetUser(dojoGone, dojoT0));
